strengths: The paper provides the first comprehensive, systematic benchmark of attentive probing/pooling methods for evaluating frozen SSL models, unifying a wide range of existing techniques (AIM, CAE, CAPI, V-JEPA, CLIP, SigLIP, CoCa, CaiT, AbMILP, DELF, SimPool, CBAM) within a single MHCA-based framework. This taxonomy and analysis is genuinely useful to the community.

The proposed EP mechanism is simple, well-motivated (removing redundant key/query projections by learning queries directly in the input feature space), and the derivation from slot attention provides useful context. The parameter/FLOP analysis is clear and correct.

Extensive and convincing evaluation: 7 classification benchmarks, 4 MIM frameworks plus JEA/hybrid/vision-language models, multiple backbone sizes, accuracy-vs-parameter and accuracy-vs-GFLOP Pareto analyses, low-shot (5%/10%) and layer-wise probing experiments, and thorough ablations (WK, WV, number of queries, Da, Do).

The analysis connecting per-predictor localization quality (bounding-box attention mass, entropy) to per-predictor importance for classification is an interesting empirical finding that goes beyond raw accuracy reporting.
The paper is well written with clear formalism, and the supplementary material is extensive (implementation details, additional datasets/backbones, visualizations), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: EP amounts to learning M query vectors in the raw patch-token space (attention computed as X^T u_j), which is a straightforward extension of AbMILP to multiple queries and a stripped-down slot attention. The technical contribution is thin; the paper's value rests mainly on the benchmark and empirical analysis.

Missing comparisons to closely related parameter-efficient adaptation methods. The appendix discusses PEFT (LoRA, VPT, BitFit, norm-tuning, adapters) but never empirically compares EP against them. Since EP's selling point is accuracy-per-parameter for frozen backbones, comparison with even the simplest selective methods (e.g., bias/norm tuning) is needed to substantiate claims of superiority in this regime.

The absolute accuracy gap to fine-tuning remains substantial (e.g., 75.6% EP vs 83.6% FT for MAE ViT-B on ImageNet), and on stronger pretrained models (SigLIP2, DINOv2) the marginal gain of EP over LP is small (~0.2–0.8%). The claim that EP 'narrows the gap to FT' holds mainly for MIM models where LP is weak.

Many headline results are presented only as figures (Figure 3, 9) with crowded scatter plots; exact numbers for all competitor methods are hard to extract, and several key comparisons lack tables. Some supplementary text contains typos/inconsistencies (e.g., 'EP16 with Do = Do/2', 'CAiT' vs 'CaiT'), suggesting limited polish.

Hyperparameter fairness concerns: learning rate is exhaustively searched per model/dataset on smaller datasets but fixed to 0.1 on ImageNet/Places365 for cost reasons; probing performance can be sensitive to this, and it is unclear whether all competitors received equally careful tuning. 90 epochs of probing training is also relatively expensive given the paper's efficiency motivation.

The 'localization correlates with importance' analysis is correlational on ImageNet validation data with ground-truth boxes; causal claims about shortcut avoidance and robustness are not directly tested (e.g., no background/robustness benchmark).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: the benchmark covers four MIM frameworks (MAE, SimMIM, BEiTv2, CAPI), multiple backbones (ViT-S/B/L), seven classification datasets, and additional pretraining paradigms (joint-embedding, hybrid, vision-language), which is more thorough than typical probing papers.

The unified framework formalizing existing attentive probing/pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, SimPool, CLIP, CoCa, etc.) as instances of a common attentive-pooling abstraction is a useful contribution for comparing methods on equal footing.

Interesting analysis connecting attention localization quality/entropy to the contribution of each predictor to classification accuracy (Section 4.4), plus ablations on the necessity of key/value projections (WK, WV) that support the design rationale.

Useful secondary results: layer-wise probing (Table 2 shows EP unlocks much more information from intermediate layers than LP) and low-shot probing (Table 3), which demonstrate practical value beyond the accuracy-parameter trade-off.
The method is simple, lightweight (only DiM parameters for attention), and the flexibility of tuning M and Do is a practical advantage for parameter-constrained settings.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contribution. Efficient probing (EP) amounts to removing the key/query projections from standard multi-head cross-attention and directly using multiple learnable query vectors dotted with frozen patch features (Eq. 10). This is a fairly incremental simplification of well-known attention pooling, and the authors themselves acknowledge the close connection to slot attention, AbMILP (EP with M=1), and AIM. The main novelty is the systematization and the benchmark rather than the mechanism itself.

The claimed significance of the accuracy gains is questionable. On the main results (Figure 3, Table 1), EP is mostly 'on par' with prior state of the art (CAE, AIM, V-JEPA) at lower parameter counts; the largest advertised gains (+13.6% over LP, Table 1) are on SimMIM ViT-B, where absolute accuracy is very low (65.1%), suggesting the gain partly reflects the weakness of the baseline rather than a fundamental improvement.

Contestable positioning claims. The paper claims to conduct 'the first systematic benchmark of attentive probing methods,' but related work (e.g., [40], 'Beyond [CLS]: Exploring the true potential of masked image modeling representations') already investigates non-CLS evaluation of MIM representations; the distinction is not clearly argued.

No comparison against parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) alternatives. The appendix reviews LoRA, VPT, AdaptFormer, etc., yet the experiments never compare EP against these established low-parameter adaptation methods, which are the natural competitors when the motivating claim is that fine-tuning is 'unsustainable.'

The localization-analysis conclusions (Section 4.4, Figure 5) may partially be a property of the frozen MAE backbone rather than of the probing method, since the attention maps are computed on frozen features; the causal interpretation ('EP produces interpretable attention maps that focus on foreground objects') is supported mainly by qualitative visualizations (Figures 6, 10-13) on a small set of images.

Some over-claiming in language ('spectacular gains,' 'remarkable robustness,' 'consistently outperforms') that is stronger than the evidence; the evaluation is restricted to classification, so claims about generality of the representation quality are broader than what is measured.

Reproducibility details are partially deferred (supplementary material for several method variants and dataset details), and key hyperparameter choices (e.g., 90 epochs, LARS, LR search) are given only at a high level; no code release is mentioned.

Statistical rigor: results appear to be single-run top-1 accuracies without variance or significance tests, which matters for the many comparisons where differences between methods are small (e.g., 75.6% vs. 74.9% for CAE).

strengths: The paper provides the first systematic, unified framework for attentive probing/pooling methods, casting a wide range of approaches (AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, AbMILP, SimPool, CLIP, CoCa, CaiT, DELF, CBAM, etc.) as variants of a generic MHCA formulation. This unifying analysis is genuinely useful for the community and clearly explains design differences among prior methods.

The proposed efficient probing (EP) is well-motivated: removing key/value projections and using learnable queries directly in the input feature space is simple, yet the paper empirically justifies why this works (e.g., the ablation showing multi-head MHCA degrades without W_K: 75.1% -> 72.9%, while EP avoids this issue).

Evaluation is extensive: seven classification benchmarks, four MIM frameworks, multiple backbone sizes (ViT-S/B/L), many competitor methods, plus supplementary experiments on joint-embedding, hybrid, and vision-language models, low-shot and layer-wise probing settings. Pareto-frontier analysis over both parameters and FLOPs is a good way to frame the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

The analysis connecting attention localization quality/entropy to per-predictor importance (Figure 5) and the visualization of query specialization (Figure 6) add interpretability value beyond raw accuracy numbers.

Useful empirical findings: EP narrows the LP-to-FT gap, reverses some k-NN/LP rankings (e.g., MAE surpassing BYOL), and shows large gains at earlier layers (+23.8% at layer 6), which is interesting for the SSL evaluation literature.
weaknesses: Novelty of the core mechanism is limited. EP (learnable query vectors dot-producted with frozen patch tokens, followed by weighted pooling) is very close to slot attention (acknowledged by the authors as a 'lightweight counterpart' with a single iteration) and to attention-based pooling with learnable queries that has been used in various forms. The contribution is more an empirical simplification/benchmarking exercise than a new technique.

The main results are presented almost entirely through scatter plots (Figures 1, 3, 4, 9) without tabulated numbers, error bars, or seed variance. Since many EP/competitor points are clustered, it is hard to verify claimed margins; single-run results on validation sets (rather than test sets) weaken the strength of conclusions.

The headline efficiency claim (up to 10x speed-up) is somewhat narrow: it compares against a full ViT block / vanilla MHCA probing, and the parameter counts include classifier parameters, which complicates the comparison. Also, EP64 achieves 'competitive' but not clearly superior accuracy in several settings (e.g., SimMIM, Food-101, CUB200 where SigLIP remains ahead), so 'on par with SOTA' claims are occasionally overstated.

Despite the related-work discussion of PEFT (LoRA, BitFit, VPT, AdaptFormer, etc. in Appendix A), the main benchmark does not empirically compare EP against these parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines, which are natural competitors for the same practical use case (adapting frozen backbones cheaply).

Some presentations issues and inconsistencies: repeated typos ('Do = Do/2' in Appendix C.2, 'Figure 9a and Figure 9a'), CAiT/SigLIP/CoCa descriptions are kept only in the appendix, and the EP-to-slot-attention derivation is informal. Also, probing still requires 90 epochs of training per task, which partially undercuts the 'unsustainability of fine-tuning' motivation without a discussion of total compute versus FT.

The causal interpretation of the localization-accuracy correlation (Figure 5) is suggestive rather than established; correlation between predictor importance and localization could arise for other reasons, and no intervention beyond the uniform-attention replacement is analyzed.

strengths: The paper presents the first systematic benchmark of attentive probing methods, unifying a diverse set of techniques (AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, CLIP, SimPool, AbMILP, DELF, etc.) under a single formal framework (Table 1), which is a genuinely useful contribution for the representation-evaluation community.

The proposed method (EP) is simple, well-motivated, and clearly derived: the framework analysis naturally leads to removing key/query projections and learning queries directly in the input feature space, reducing parameters and compute while matching or beating heavier prior methods.

The evaluation is extensive and thorough: 15 pre-trained backbones spanning five paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, generative), seven datasets, accuracy-vs-parameters and accuracy-vs-FLOPs Pareto analyses, low-shot and layer-wise probing, and ablations on W_K, W_V, number of queries, D_a, and D_o.

Interesting empirical analysis beyond accuracy: the correlation between attention localization quality and per-predictor accuracy contribution (Figure 4), and the complementarity metric showing EP's queries specialize in distinct object regions (Figures 5-6, 11), with reasonable controls (all 12 blocks, max vs. average similarity, matched predictor counts).

The supplementary extensions (Matryoshka-style multi-scale probing, attention mixing) and honest limitations section add value; the findings that EP reshapes the ranking of pre-training methods (e.g., MAE surpassing BYOL, CAPI surpassing CLIP) are meaningful for the evaluation-protocol debate.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: EP is essentially a stripped-down multi-query cross-attention (learnable queries with identity key transform), closely related to slot attention (single iteration, no GRU/LN/MLP) and AbMILP; the paper acknowledges this, and the conceptual contribution is mostly a simplification rather than a new mechanism.

Gains over linear probing are modest for the strongest recent models (DINOv2 +0.4-0.8, DINOv3 +0.4-0.5, SigLIP2 +1.8), so the practical impact is concentrated on models with weaker global tokens (SimMIM, DiT, MAE), narrowing the scope of the headline claim that EP 'narrows the gap to fine-tuning'.

The claim that sharper/foreground-focused attention causes accuracy gains is only correlational; Figure 4 shows a relationship between localization and per-predictor accuracy contribution but no causal evidence, and interpretability claims rely largely on qualitative visualizations.

Some experimental details raise fairness questions: the LR search range [0.1, 5.0] is applied per model on small datasets but fixed to 0.1 on ImageNet-1K for cost reasons, and the 90-epoch schedule may advantage methods tuned to it; the 'first comprehensive study' claim would be strengthened by sensitivity analysis of the protocol itself.

No explicit statement of code release, which limits reproducibility of the benchmark; also, evaluation is confined to image classification (acknowledged), and key auxiliary analyses (Matryoshka, attention mixing) are only run on a single model/dataset.

Minor presentation issues: some figures (e.g., Figure 2, 8, 13) are dense and hard to parse; text occasionally overstates ('remarkable', 'emerging properties') relative to the simplicity of the technique.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmarking: the paper evaluates a large set of attentive pooling/probing methods (15+ methods) across 15 pre-trained models spanning five paradigms and seven datasets, which is a genuinely useful empirical contribution to the community.

The unified framework (Sec. 3.1–3.2, Table 1) that recasts existing methods (AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, AbMILP, DELF, SimPool, etc.) as variants of a common attentive-pooling template is clear and pedagogically valuable.
Extensive ablations and analyses: layer-wise probing, low-shot probing, effect of M/Da/Do, Matryoshka probing, attention complementarity metrics, and many qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
The method is simple and well-motivated; the connection to slot attention and the analysis of when a single learnable query can absorb WK are informative.
Results are broadly consistent: EP sits on or near the Pareto frontier across many settings, with large gains for MIM/generative models (e.g., DiT +24.3%).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: EP is essentially learnable query vectors dotted with raw frozen features, which is a simplification of existing multi-head cross-attention (and of slot attention / AbMILP with multiple queries). Removing WQ and WK is a straightforward parameter reduction rather than a new idea; the paper itself admits EP is a 'lightweight counterpart of slot attention' with a single iteration.

The efficiency framing can overstate the contribution: relative to the most natural baseline (linear probing with [CLS]), EP uses more parameters (1.4M vs 0.8M on ViT-B) and the headline gains are largest exactly where LP is weakest (MIM/generative models), which is a known phenomenon (cf. Przewiezlikowski et al., 2024, which the paper cites). The claim of a 'first comprehensive study' partially overlaps this prior work.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable in places: the learning-rate search range is fixed to 0.1 for the large-scale datasets to save compute, which could disadvantage heavier competitor methods; several baselines (CaiT, SigLIP, CoCa, CLIP) are re-implementations/repurposings whose tuning is not thoroughly validated.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the 'complementary attention maps' finding rests on a custom, self-defined complementarity metric that is never validated against an external criterion, and the semantic specialization of queries (tails, beaks, feet) is supported only by a handful of qualitative visualizations on bird images.
No error bars, seed variance, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, despite accuracy differences between EP and the best competitors (AIM/MHCA) being small in many plots.

Analysis in Figure 4 establishes only a correlation between localization quality and accuracy contribution; the causal narrative ('not shortcut learning') is asserted but not established, and the paper does not test robustness claims experimentally despite claiming improved robustness.

Significance of the contribution to a broad AI audience is limited: the scope is evaluation-protocol design for vision backbones, and the paper offers no theory; the practical impact of a ~1-3 point probing gain at slightly higher parameter count is debatable.

Writing issues: several typos/grammatical errors (e.g., 'are benefit the most', 'methods like as DINOv2'), and some key experimental details (e.g., how Do is reduced relative to classifier parameters) require careful digging to verify.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: probing protocols (especially [CLS]-based linear probing) under-utilize patch-token representations of MIM, AR, and diffusion models; the accuracy-vs-parameter-efficiency lens is a sensible and underexplored angle.

The unified framework (Sec. 3, Table 1) that casts many existing attentive pooling methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP, CAiT, SigLIP, CAE, CoCa) as variants of one attention-pooling template is genuinely useful and makes the design-space comparison systematic rather than anecdotal.

EP is extremely simple (learnable queries in the full feature space, no key projections), and the ablations (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 13) properly validate the two key design decisions: removing W_K is fine for single-head but not multi-head, and W_V is critical for all methods.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 15 backbones spanning five pre-training paradigms, seven datasets, Pareto-frontier analysis over parameters and GFLOPs, plus layer-wise probing, low-shot probing, Matryoshka probing, and attention-mixing extensions.

The analysis beyond raw accuracy (localization-accuracy correlation, attention complementarity metric, entropy analysis) adds scientific value and suggests EP's queries act as implicit part detectors; the appendix carefully addresses obvious objections (e.g., complementarity across all 12 blocks, SigLIP cross-attention control).
Honest limitations section and transparent LLM-use statement; broad availability of details (optimizer, LR search, batch sizes, hardware) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: EP is essentially AbMILP/slot-attention extended to multiple queries with the key projection removed; the paper itself concedes it is a 'lightweight counterpart of slot attention'. The contribution is closer to a well-executed empirical study + simplification than a new technique.

The 'first comprehensive study of attentive probing' claim is somewhat overstated: prior work such as Przewiezlikowski et al. (2024) 'Beyond [CLS]' already explores probing MIM representations beyond the CLS token, and it is cited but not compared against empirically.

No variance reporting: single-run results, no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which matters given that many reported gains (e.g., +0.4 to +0.8 for DINOv3/Franca/DINOv2 in Table 2) are small and could be within run-to-run noise. LR search was also fixed at 0.1 for large datasets, which may disadvantage some baselines.

Evaluation is confined to image classification; claims about EP's complementarity, robustness, and interpretability are only validated on classification with qualitative attention visualizations and a self-defined complementarity metric whose practical significance is not established (no downstream task actually benefits from complementarity in the paper).

Several headline comparisons are somewhat favorable by construction: FT numbers are often taken from official papers under different setups, some LP baselines use GAP-based numbers, and EP variants are tuned over M and D_o per setting, whereas baselines get less configuration search; the claim of 'state-of-the-art' rests on these protocol choices.

Impact is moderate: EP improves probing accuracy for frozen-backbone evaluation, a niche but relevant protocol; it does not change how models are trained, and the paper leaves the more interesting directions (interaction with PEFT, dense tasks, pre-stored feature protocol) as future work.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed benchmark: the paper systematically unifies a wide range of attentive pooling/probing methods (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CAE, CAPI, CLIP, SigLIP, CaiT, CoCa, CBAM, etc.) under a single MHCA-based framework, and evaluates them across 15 backbones spanning five pre-training paradigms and seven datasets - a genuinely useful contribution to the community for the first time.

The proposed method (EP) is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: replacing per-head key projections with learnable queries directly in the input feature space is a clean parameter reduction that is mathematically equivalent to MHCA, and the paper carefully verifies this equivalence empirically (identical accuracy at matched head count with far fewer parameters).

Strong and diverse empirical support: accuracy-parameter and accuracy-FLOPs Pareto analysis, comparisons against more than 40 LoRA/PEFT configurations showing EP is complementary (LoRA+EP dominates both), low-shot probing, layer-wise probing, cross-dataset k-NN generalization, zero-shot retrieval, and WSOL localization - the claims are backed by a broad set of experiments.

Thoughtful analysis section: the correlation between attention localization quality and accuracy contribution, complementarity metrics across backbones and methods, entropy analysis, Matryoshka multi-scale probing, and attention-mixing ablations add scientific insight beyond just pushing accuracy.

Well-written and honest: limitations are explicitly discussed (frozen backbones only, classification focus, diagnostic nature of complementarity analysis), the LLM usage statement is present, and overclaiming is mostly avoided.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: EP is essentially slot attention reduced to a single iteration with learnable slots (acknowledged by the authors), or a learnable-query variant of existing attentive probing with the key projection removed; the contribution is more a simplification and systematic study than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Gains over the strongest existing attentive probing baselines (e.g., AIM/MHCA at matched accuracy) are primarily in parameter count rather than accuracy, and in some regimes (e.g., DINOv2/DINOv3, SigLIP2) the EP improvement over linear probing is small (+0.4 to +0.5), so the practical impact depends heavily on the backbone choice.

Evaluation is limited to image classification for the main results; downstream tasks such as detection and segmentation are only mentioned as future work, and no statistical significance/error bars are reported for the 90-epoch probing runs despite some reported differences being small.

The fixed hyperparameter space (M, Do) requires per-configuration search, and the reported 'state-of-the-art' configurations are cherry-picked points on the Pareto front; a clearer practical recipe for choosing M and Do for a new backbone would strengthen reproducibility.

The 'first comprehensive study' claim, while largely defensible, is slightly overstated given related concurrent work on probing MIM representations (e.g., Przewikezlikowski et al., 2025, which the authors do cite).

strengths: The paper offers the first unified framework for attentive probing methods, mapping a diverse set of prior approaches (AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA, CLIP-style pooling, etc.) onto a common formulation (Table 1), which is a genuinely useful contribution for the community.

The experimental coverage is unusually broad: 15 pre-trained backbones spanning five paradigms, seven datasets, comparisons against PEFT (LoRA sweeps, BitFit, LayerNorm tuning), layer-wise probing, low-shot regimes, zero-shot retrieval, and unsupervised localization, plus extensive ablations (W_K, W_V, number of queries M, output dimensionality D_o).

The analysis section is thoughtful: the correlation between attention localization quality and per-predictor accuracy contribution, the complementarity metric, and the demonstration that EP224/EP12 matches mathematically equivalent MHCA with fewer parameters are informative.
The supplementary material is thorough (Matryoshka probing, attention mixing, convergence analysis, limitations), and the writing is generally clear.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited. EP is essentially a reparameterization of existing multi-head cross-attention probing (e.g., AIM): absorbing W_K into learnable queries in the input feature space is a standard matrix-factorization trick, and the authors themselves prove the equivalence to MHCA with the same head count. The 'method' contribution is a simplification of prior work rather than a new mechanism.

Gains over linear probing on strong modern backbones are marginal (e.g., DINOv3 +0.4-0.5%, DINOv2 +0.4-0.8%, iBOT +0.5%), while the headline numbers (+17-24%) come from weak backbones (MAE ViT-S, SimMIM, DiT) where any patch-token aggregation was already known to help. The paper's significance claim rests heavily on these weak-backbone cases.

No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds, no error bars, and many reported differences between methods (e.g., EP vs. AIM at matched M) are within 0.1-0.5%, which could easily be noise. The learning-rate search protocol is also inconsistent (exhaustive search on small datasets, fixed LR=0.1 on ImageNet-1K/Places365), which weakens fairness of the accuracy-efficiency comparisons.

The parameter-efficiency framing is partly misleading: the best EP results (EP32/EP64/EP128) use more trainable parameters than linear probing on the same backbone, and the most accurate all-layer LoRA configurations actually surpass EP in accuracy (76.7% vs 75.6%); the 'dominance' claim depends on a particular choice of parameter budget axes.

Several presentation/consistency issues undermine polish: Table 6 mislabels the baseline attention column as 'LP'; typos such as 'Do = Do/2' and 'EP16' vs 'EP12' discrepancies; garbled table formatting (Tables 10-11). The complementarity metric is ad hoc and somewhat circular, since externally learned queries trained solely for classification would naturally diverge, and no evidence is given that complementarity causes (rather than merely correlates with) performance.
No code release is stated anywhere, which is a significant reproducibility concern for a paper whose main selling point is a benchmark of many methods.

The positioning as 'probing as evaluation protocol' is in tension with the PEFT comparison: EP modifies the probing procedure with learned queries, so the measured accuracy is no longer a pure measure of representation quality, blurring the paper's stated motivation.

strengths: The paper presents the first systematic and comprehensive benchmark of attentive probing methods, unifying a wide range of prior approaches (AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, CAPI, AbMILP, DELF, SimPool, CLIP, SigLIP, CoCa, CaiT, CBAM, etc.) within a single attentive-pooling framework. This unified view is genuinely useful for the community and makes the design space easy to reason about.

Evaluation is extensive and convincing: 15 pre-trained models spanning five paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLM, generative), 7 datasets spanning large-scale, fine-grained, and scene-centric settings, plus PEFT comparisons (LoRA, BitFit, LayerNorm tuning), low-shot probing, layer-wise probing, zero-shot retrieval, and WSOL localization. The appendix contains thorough ablations (W_K/W_V roles, M, D_a, D_o, Matryoshka probing, attention mixing, convergence).

The proposed EP method is simple, well-motivated, and the mathematical equivalence analysis (absorbing W_K into learnable queries in the full feature space) is clean. The empirical Pareto analysis in accuracy-vs-parameters and accuracy-vs-GFLOPs clearly supports the efficiency claim.

The comparison against PEFT is a notable strength: the finding that LoRA+EP strictly dominates both pure EP and pure LoRA, plus the cross-dataset k-NN analysis showing EP preserves representations better than LoRA, is an interesting and practically relevant result.

The analysis of attention quality (localization/entropy vs. per-predictor accuracy contribution) and the complementarity metric provide insight beyond raw accuracy, and the diagnostic treatment (e.g., the auxiliary similarity-loss experiment showing EP learns complementarity without an explicit loss) is honest and well designed.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. EP essentially reduces to M learnable query vectors dot-multiplied against raw patch tokens followed by value-weighted aggregation — a natural simplification of MHCA with a learnable query, closely related to slot attention (single iteration, no LN/GRU/MLP) and to multi-query AbMILP. The paper's own equivalence analysis confirms AIM12 and EP12 attain identical accuracy; the contribution is thus mostly a parameter-count reduction rather than a new capability.

Absolute gains over existing attentive probing are often small for strong backbones (e.g., +0.4–0.5% for DINOv2/DINOv3, +0.4–0.5% for iBOT). Headline numbers like '+24.3%' come from weak baselines (DiT [CLS]), which somewhat overstates the practical impact for models where probing matters most.
No variance reporting: results appear to be single runs with no seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, which matters when differences of 0.2–0.5% are used to claim Pareto dominance.

The fixed 90-epoch protocol for all methods may disadvantage computationally heavier competitors (e.g., V-JEPA, ViT block) or under-tune them; the LR search range and schedule choices could favor EP, and fairness of the training budget across method families deserves more scrutiny.

The claim that 'the accuracy of methods whose pre-training optimizes patch-token representations benefits most' is supported observationally (entropy analysis) but remains correlational; a more controlled causal analysis is lacking.

Reproducibility details are only partially provided (no explicit code release statement); given the benchmark-centric contribution, releasing the unified framework and per-method configurations would substantially increase the paper's value.
